description: Daedalus makes wax wings to escape Crete. His son Icarus flies too high, falls and gives his name to a sea. A myth about measure and excess.

hero.hook: A father invents wings. A son ignores the warning. The sea keeps its name.

blocks.text: **Icarus** and his father **Daedalus** form one of the best-known Greek myths. Beyond the image of the teenager who falls into the sea, the story speaks of ingenuity, limits and the temptation to go too far.
It's the story of an impossible escape that becomes a lesson in : to want to equal the gods is to risk getting burned. [[Hybris and excess]]

**Daedalus** is a legendary inventor, incarnation of , this cunning intelligence of the Greeks. Exiled to the court of King **Minos**, in Crete, he built the **Labyrinth**, a prison so complex that no one escapes. She hides the **Minotaur**, a monster born from the forbidden loves of Queen . [[Metis]] [[Pasiphae]]

blocks.caption: Daedalus, architect of the Cretan Labyrinth.

blocks.text: When Minos learns that Daedalus helped the hero **Theseus** to escape thanks to Ariadne's thread, he locks the inventor and his young son **Icarus** in their own work. Lands and seas are locked. There remains the sky.
The French word **“maze”** comes from this character: a place where one gets lost, like the Labyrinth he designed.
While observing the birds, Daedalus makes two pairs of wings: wood, feathers and **wax** bee. Technology becomes a way out.

sections.title: Daedalus, prisoner of his own labyrinth

blocks.text: Before leaving, Daedalus gives Icarus a simple rule: follow the middle path. Too low, the humidity weighs down the feathers. Too high, the sun melts the wax. This prudence recalls , the wisdom of knowing one's place. [[Sophia]]

At first, everything is fine. Father and son fly over the islands of the Aegean Sea. The shepherds on the ground believe they see gods. Then drunkenness seizes Icarus. He rises, fascinated by the sky. The wax softens. The feathers fall. He flaps his bare arms and dives into the sea.

blocks.caption: The fall of Icarus, subject of painting since the Renaissance.

blocks.text: The myth is scientifically paradoxical: the higher you go, the colder it gets. Icarus should have frozen rather than see his wax melt.

sections.title: Fly too high, or too low

blocks.text: The Elders see above all a punishment for pride: Icarus pays for having wanted too much. But romantics, like **Baudelaire**, make him a hero of the ideal: it is better to die looking at the sun than a cautious life on the ground.

The painter **Pieter Bruegel the Elder** offers another reading. In his painting, the fall is only a detail: the plowman continues his task, the world does not stop for a hero. The individual feat becomes almost invisible.
Some versions add that Daedalus also sees the death of his son as a punishment: once, out of jealousy, he would have killed his nephew **Perdix**, an overly gifted inventor.

The currents carry Icarus' body towards an island that the hero **Heracles** names . The surrounding sea becomes the **[[Ikaria]]n Sea**. Daedalus, alone, reaches Sicily and offers his wings to the god **Apollo**, swearing never to fly again.

The myth survives everywhere: in aeronautics as a dream and risk, in psychology as the “Icarus complex”, the desire to succeed too quickly. Daedalus remains the ambiguous inventor, capable of the best (the wings) as well as the worst.  reminds us that technology can also confine people. [[The labyrinth as a symbol]]
**Daedalus** flees Crete with wings of wax. **Icarus** ignores the warning, flies too close to the sun and drowns. Technology liberates, but without measure it kills.
